name: How do I make a small Los Angeles bathroom accessible without expanding the footprint?

mainEntity.name: How can an accessible bathroom remodel work in a tiny LA bathroom where the tub, toilet, and vanity are all packed together?
mainEntity.text: How can an accessible bathroom remodel work in a tiny LA bathroom where the tub, toilet, and vanity are all packed together?

acceptedAnswer.text: In a compact Los Angeles bathroom, accessibility usually starts with space planning, not product selection. A good remodel may keep the existing footprint while changing fixture placement, removing the tub, and choosing a curbless shower with a linear drain. Wall-mounted vanities, pocket doors, and offset toilets can free up room for turning and side transfers. The key is to preserve a clear path from the door to the sink, toilet, and shower without creating pinch points. If the layout is tight, a designer or contractor should measure turning radius, shower entry width, and grab-bar placement before finalizing finishes. Homeowners often assume accessibility requires a full addition, but many bathrooms can be adapted within the same square footage if the layout is efficient. The tradeoff is that some features, such as a larger shower or dual sinks, may need to be reduced or removed to meet accessibility goals.
acceptedAnswer.description: A small bathroom can be made accessible by replacing a tub with a low-threshold or curbless shower, widening the clear floor area, using a wall-mounted or compact vanity, and relocating fixtures to improve turning space. The goal is not just adding grab bars, but creating usable circulation and safe transfer zones.
